title: Poiseuille's Formula for Viscous Flow
short_intro: Poiseuille's formula describes the laminar, steady-state flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid through a long cylindrical pipe of constant circular cross-section. It establishes that the volume flow rate is directly proportional to the pressure gradient and the fourth power of the radius of the pipe.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct application of Poiseuille's formula for volume flow rate, dependence on radius, length, viscosity, and pressure difference, along with units and dimensional verification.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation using Navier-Stokes equation in cylindrical coordinates, hydrodynamic resistance analogy to Ohm's law, and series/parallel combination of capillary tubes.

prerequisites: Laminar versus turbulent flow and Reynolds number

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Flow and Velocity Profile
bullets: The fluid flow must be steady, streamline (laminar), and incompressible with negligible entrance effects.
The velocity profile across the cross-section of a cylindrical pipe is parabolic, with maximum velocity at the axis and zero velocity at the inner wall due to the no-slip condition.
The velocity v(r) at a radial distance r from the axis is given by v(r) = &frac{Delta P}{4eta l} (R2 - r2).

concept_notes.heading: Dependence on Physical Parameters
bullets: Volume flow rate Q is directly proportional to the pressure difference (ΔP) and the fourth power of the radius (R4).
Volume flow rate Q is inversely proportional to the coefficient of viscosity (η) and the length of the pipe (l).
A small change in the radius of a blood vessel or pipe leads to a massive fourth-power change in the flow rate, highlighting the sensitivity of hydrodynamic resistance.

concept_notes.heading: Analogy with Electrical Circuits
bullets: Poiseuille's law can be expressed in a form analogous to Ohm's Law (I = V/R), where volume flow rate Q acts as current and pressure difference ΔP acts as potential difference.
Hydrodynamic resistance Rh of a cylindrical pipe is defined as Rh = &frac{8eta l}{pi R4}.
For pipes connected in series, equivalent resistance is the sum of individual resistances; for parallel connections, reciprocals add up.

concept_notes.heading: Limitations and Validity Conditions
bullets: The formula is valid only for streamline (laminar) flow where the Reynolds number remains well below the critical value (typically < 2000).
The fluid must be Newtonian, meaning its viscosity remains constant regardless of the shear rate applied.
The tube must be rigid, cylindrical, and sufficiently long so that end effects and velocity profile development length can be ignored.

derivations.title: Derivation of Poiseuille's Equation using Force Balance
derivations.conditions: Steady, laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a horizontal cylindrical pipe of radius R and length l under a pressure difference ΔP.
steps: Consider a cylindrical fluid element of radius r and length dx coaxial with the pipe.
The driving force due to pressure difference acting on the cross-section is (ΔP) (πr^2).
The opposing viscous drag force acting on the curved surface of the fluid cylinder is -(η)(2πr dx)(dv/dr).
Equating the driving force and viscous drag for steady uniform flow: (ΔP)(πr^2) = -2πr η dx (dv/dr), leading to dv/dr = -(ΔP/(2η l)) r.
Integrating with the no-slip boundary condition v = 0 at r = R gives the velocity profile v(r) = (ΔP/(4η l))(R^2 - r^2).
Integrating the elementary volume flux dQ = v(r) (2πr dr) from r = 0 to r = R yields the total volume flow rate.
derivations.result: Q =  rac{pi (Delta P) R^4}{8 eta l}

derivations.title: Derivation of Hydrodynamic Resistance
derivations.conditions: Analogy between fluid flow and current electricity.
steps: Start with Poiseuille's formula: Q =  rac{pi R^4 Delta P}{8 eta l}.
Rearrange the equation to isolate the pressure difference: ΔP = Q left( rac{8 eta l}{pi R^4}ight).
Compare this equation with Ohm's Law V = I R_elec, where V corresponds to ΔP and I corresponds to Q.
Identify the term inside the parenthesis as the hydrodynamic resistance R_h.

formula_sheet.name: Poiseuille's Law (Volume Flow Rate)
formula_sheet.equation_html: Q =  rac{pi Delta P R^4}{8 eta l}
formula_sheet.variables: Q = Volume flow rate, ΔP = Pressure difference, R = Radius, η = Coefficient of viscosity, l = Length
formula_sheet.units: Q in m^3/s, ΔP in Pa, R and l in m, η in Pa·s
formula_sheet.conditions: Laminar flow, Newtonian fluid, rigid cylindrical pipe

formula_sheet.name: Velocity Profile in Pipe
formula_sheet.equation_html: v(r) =  rac{Delta P}{4 eta l} (R^2 - r^2)
formula_sheet.variables: v(r) = Velocity at radius r, r = Radial distance from axis
formula_sheet.units: v in m/s, r in m

formula_sheet.name: Maximum Velocity
formula_sheet.equation_html: v_{max} =  rac{Delta P R^2}{4 eta l}
formula_sheet.variables: v_{max} = Velocity at the central axis (r = 0)
formula_sheet.conditions: At the axis of the pipe

formula_sheet.name: Average Velocity
formula_sheet.equation_html: v_{avg} =  rac{Q}{pi R^2} =  rac{Delta P R^2}{8 eta l} =  rac{v_{max}}{2}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Profile across Pipe Cross-section
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve showing velocity on the horizontal axis and radial distance r (from -R to +R) on the vertical axis, with maximum velocity at r = 0 and zero at the walls.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that fluid layers move fastest at the center and slowest at the stationary boundaries due to viscous shearing.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions identifying the shape of velocity distribution in laminar flow.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Volume Flow Rate Q versus Radius R
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A steeply rising non-linear curve representing Q proportional to R^4.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the extreme sensitivity of flow rate to the radius of the pipe.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problem-solving where radius is doubled or halved and the resulting change in Q is calculated.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Capillary Flow Viscometer Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic setup showing a liquid reservoir, a horizontal capillary tube of known length and radius, a manometer or liquid column measuring pressure head, and a measuring cylinder.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to experimentally determine the coefficient of viscosity (η) of a liquid by measuring Q and ΔP.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Experimental physics viva and conceptual questions on measuring dynamic viscosity.

solved_numericals.question: A liquid flows through a capillary tube of radius 1 mm and length 10 cm under a pressure head equivalent to 20 cm of water column. If the radius of the tube is doubled keeping all other parameters constant, find the ratio of the new volume flow rate to the original volume flow rate.
solution_steps: Poiseuille's formula states that volume flow rate Q is proportional to R^4 when ΔP, η, and l are constant.
Given that R_2 = 2 R_1, substitute the ratio into the expression: Q_2 / Q_1 = (2 R_1 / R_1)^4 = 2^4 = 16.

solved_numericals.question: Two capillary tubes of radii r and 2r, and lengths l and 2l respectively, are connected in series. If the pressure difference across the combination is P, find the pressure drop across the first tube.
solution_steps: Calculate the hydrodynamic resistance of the first tube: R_1 = 8ηl / (π r^4).
Calculate the hydrodynamic resistance of the second tube: R_2 = 8η(2l) / (π (2r)^4) = 16ηl / (16π r^4) = ηl / (π r^4) = R_1 / 8.
Equivalent resistance for series combination: R_eq = R_1 + R_2 = R_1 + (R_1 / 8) = (9/8) R_1.
The pressure drop across the first tube (ΔP_1) is given by Q * R_1, and since Q = P / R_eq, we have ΔP_1 = P * (R_1 / R_eq) = P * (R_1 / ((9/8) R_1)) = (8/9) P.

solved_numericals.question: Water at 20°C (viscosity η = 1.0 × 10^-3 Pa·s) flows through a pipe of radius 2.0 cm and length 2.0 m at a volume flow rate of 3.14 × 10^-4 m^3/s. Calculate the pressure difference maintaining this flow.
solution_steps: Write Poiseuille's formula for pressure difference: ΔP =  rac{8 eta l Q}{pi R^4}.
Substitute the given values: η = 1.0 × 10^-3 Pa·s, l = 2.0 m, Q = 3.14 × 10^-4 m^3/s, R = 0.02 m.
Substitute into the expression: ΔP =  rac{8 	imes (1.0 	imes 10^{-3}) 	imes 2.0 	imes (3.14 	imes 10^{-4})}{3.14 	imes (1.6 	imes 10^{-7})}.
Simplify the numerator: 8 	imes 2.0 	imes 3.14 	imes 10^{-7} = 50.24 	imes 10^{-7}.
Simplify the denominator: 3.14 	imes 1.6 	imes 10^{-7} = 5.024 	imes 10^{-7}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The fluid is strictly Newtonian and incompressible. Limitation: Fails for non-Newtonian fluids like blood under certain shear rates or polymer solutions.
Assumption: Flow is completely laminar. Limitation: If velocity exceeds the critical Reynolds number, turbulence sets in and Poiseuille's law becomes invalid.
Assumption: The pipe is rigid and has a uniform circular cross-section. Limitation: Fails in elastic vessels (like arteries) that expand with pressure or pipes with varying diameters.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Volume flow rate is inversely proportional to the square of the radius.
common_misconceptions.correct: Volume flow rate is directly proportional to the fourth power of the radius (R^4).
common_misconceptions.why: Integrating the parabolic velocity profile introduces an extra r^2 factor, transforming the area dependence into R^4.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Fluid velocity is uniform across the entire cross-section of the pipe.
common_misconceptions.correct: Fluid velocity varies parabolically, being maximum at the center and zero at the walls.
common_misconceptions.why: The no-slip condition at the solid boundary combined with internal viscous shear creates a parabolic velocity gradient.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poiseuille's formula can be applied directly to turbulent flow in rough pipes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Poiseuille's formula holds exclusively for laminar flow in smooth, cylindrical pipes.
common_misconceptions.why: Turbulent flow involves eddies and momentum mixing, drastically altering the pressure drop versus flow rate relationship.

quick_revision: Poiseuille's formula: Q = (π ΔP R^4) / (8 eta l).
Hydrodynamic resistance: R_h = (8 eta l) / (π R^4).
Velocity profile is parabolic with v_max = 2 v_avg.
Flow rate depends extremely sensitively on radius as R^4.
